\chapter{One Box, Two Characters, and the First Thing You Can Refuse}
\label{ch:zh-negation}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write \zh{口} and \zh{日} -- the second being the first with one bar added -- and I can disagree in Mandarin by putting \zh{不} in front of a word I already know, because Mandarin has no standalone word for no.}

The first exchange in the book that contains a disagreement -- a greeting, a question, and a refusal built by negating a word the reader has had since the opening lesson.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kǒu]{\zh{口} — the box, on its own}

\label{lesson:ZH-W04-kou}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{四}. Walls, then the two inner strokes, then the bottom last.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{口}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Your hand can already write this.} Three strokes, in exactly the order you learned inside \zh{四}, and the rule from there is the whole instruction:

1. the \textbf{left vertical}, top to bottom 2. the \textbf{top and right side in one turning stroke} — the \emph{héngzhé}, across then down without lifting 3. the \textbf{bottom bar}, closing it — \textbf{last}

Three strokes, two pen lifts. Walls, then the door.

One honest note, because it will save you trouble later. The enclosing frame around \zh{四} and this character are \textbf{not the same piece}, even though they are written identically. Chinese has a separate enclosure component that does the surrounding, and \zh{口} is a character in its own right. What transfers here is the hand movement, not the identity — and the hand movement is most of the work.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{口} — left wall, turning stroke, bottom last
  \item \zh{四}, then \zh{口} — the same movement, two different pieces
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes? (\textbf{Three} — the turning corner counts as one.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kǒu]{\zh{口} — mouth, and a piece you will meet everywhere}

\label{lesson:ZH-C04-kou}



\begin{quote}
Draw the box. Three strokes, bottom last.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{口}} \emph{kǒu} means \textbf{mouth}.

Look at it again now that it means something. \textbf{It is an open mouth, seen from the front} — squared off, the way every Chinese character is squared off to fit its block, but a picture all the same. The oldest forms are rounder and even more obviously a mouth.

\textbf{kǒu} is \textbf{third tone}, the low dipping one you have had since \emph{nǐ}. Keep it low. {[}REPEAT x2{]}
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
You have already met pieces that live inside other characters — \zh{女} and \zh{子} sit inside \zh{好}. \zh{口} is the commonest of them all. When you see it as a \textbf{small element in a corner} of a bigger character, it very often says the word has something to do with the \textbf{mouth}: speaking, eating, calling, tasting.

The size matters. A full-height frame around a whole character is a different piece doing a different job; the mouth hint is for the small one tucked into a corner.

That is worth more than the word itself. You are not going to memorise five thousand characters as pictures; you are going to learn a few hundred pieces and read the rest as combinations. \zh{口} is one of the commonest pieces there is.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kǒu} — low and dipping
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{口} — and say what it is a picture of
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
If you meet this box inside a bigger character, what does it usually hint at? (Something to do with the \textbf{mouth}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rì]{\zh{日} — one bar inside the box}

\label{lesson:ZH-W04-ri}



\begin{quote}
Draw the box. Now hold it in your head; you are about to fill it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{日}
\end{quote}

\textbf{The same box, with one horizontal bar across the middle.} That is the entire difference, and it buys you a second character.

Four strokes, and the order has one thing worth getting right:

1. the \textbf{left vertical} 2. the \textbf{top and right side}, one turning stroke 3. the \textbf{middle bar} 4. the \textbf{bottom bar}, closing it — still last

\textbf{The middle bar goes in before the bottom.} Fill the box, then shut it. That is the same instinct as the box rule itself, applied one level in: you never close a space you still have to write inside.

Three pen lifts. If your box was comfortable, this cost you one line.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{口}, then \zh{日} — the same four movements plus one
  \item \zh{日} — and check that the middle bar went in before the bottom
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes separate this character from the box? (\textbf{One}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rì]{\zh{日} — the sun, and the day it measures}

\label{lesson:ZH-C04-ri}



\begin{quote}
Write the box, then the box with a bar. Two characters, one shape.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{日}} \emph{rì} means \textbf{sun} — and also \textbf{day}.

The picture is the sun: a disc with a mark in the middle. Squared off, like everything else, but that is what the bar is doing there. The oldest forms are a circle with a dot.

\textbf{rì} is \textbf{fourth tone}, falling. The \emph{r} is not an English \emph{r} and not a Spanish one either: start where your tongue sits for the \emph{s} in English \emph{measure}, then \textbf{curl the tip back} a little. Let the vowel be short and tight. \emph{Twice through:}
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Sun} and \textbf{day} in the same word is not a Chinese quirk. It is what happens in language after language, because the sun is how a day was counted before anybody had a clock. English does the same thing from the other end: we say \emph{the sun rose} and \emph{three days later}, and nobody finds it strange that a \emph{day} is both the light and the span.

So this is one of the rare characters where you get two meanings and have to learn neither: they are the same idea, and the context tells you which.

Like \zh{口}, this one turns up \textbf{inside} other characters, and when it does it is almost always about the sun, light, or time.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{rì} — falling, and the \emph{r} of \emph{measure}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{日} — and say both of its meanings
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
If you meet this shape inside a bigger character, what is it hinting at? (\textbf{Sun, light or time}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bù]{\zh{不} — four strokes, all of them separate}

\label{lesson:ZH-W04-bu}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{日}. Middle bar before the bottom.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{不}
\end{quote}

Four strokes, in this order:

1. a \textbf{top horizontal}, left to right 2. lift, then a \textbf{long stroke from the upper centre down to the left} 3. lift, then the \textbf{central vertical}, straight down 4. lift, then a \textbf{short right-falling dot}

\textbf{Three pen lifts, and every stroke stands alone.} Nothing joins here. That is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly: the boxes you have just written were one continuous movement in places, and this is the opposite — four deliberate, separate marks under a single roof.

The commonest beginner's version runs the second and third strokes together into a corner. They are not a corner. Lift.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \zh{不} — top bar, the long left-falling stroke, the vertical, the dot
  \item it again, counting the lifts aloud. There should be three.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do the second and third strokes meet in a corner? (\textbf{No} — lift between them.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bù]{\zh{不} — how Mandarin says no}

\label{lesson:ZH-C04-bu}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{不}, counting three lifts. Then say \textbf{hǎo} — good.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\textbf{\zh{不}} \emph{bù} means \textbf{not}.

\textbf{bù} is \textbf{fourth tone}, falling — the same firm drop you learned on \emph{èr} and \emph{sì}. {[}REPEAT x2{]}
\end{sounds}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: there is no word for \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}]
Here is something that surprises nearly every learner, and it is better met now than discovered later.

\textbf{Mandarin has no single word meaning \textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{}}

English has one. So does French, Spanish, Russian. Mandarin does not. What it has instead is \textbf{\zh{不}}, which goes in front of a word and turns it around:

\begin{quote}
\zh{好} \emph{hǎo} — good
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\zh{不好} \emph{bù hǎo} — not good
\end{quote}

So when someone asks you a yes-or-no question in Mandarin, you do not answer with a word for \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{You answer by negating the thing they asked about.} Ask whether something is \zh{好}, and \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} comes back as \zh{不好}.

This sounds like extra work and is actually less: you already know \zh{好}, so you already know how to refuse it, and the same holds for every word you have so far.

One word will break the pattern later — Mandarin has a second negator for \emph{having}, and you will meet it with the word it belongs to. Everything in this book up to now takes \zh{不}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{bù} — falling, firm
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hǎo}, then \textbf{bù hǎo} — good, then not good
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{不好}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
You have known \zh{好} since the first lesson. How much did its opposite cost you? (\textbf{One character}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — one box, two characters, and a refusal}

\label{lesson:ZH-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{口}. Then write \zh{日}. One line apart.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Two voices, using only what you have:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{你好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{ní hǎo}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{你好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{ní hǎo}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{hǎo} — good?
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{不好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{bù hǎo} — not good.
\end{quote}

Small, and it is the first time in this book you have been able to \textbf{disagree}. Up to now every exchange has been agreement: a greeting answered by the same greeting, a number read back. This one has a no in it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Three characters, and not one of them cost what it looks like it cost:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{口}} \emph{kǒu}, mouth — you already knew the shape; it is the box from the number four, standing on its own
  \item \textbf{\zh{日}} \emph{rì}, sun and day — the same box with one bar added
  \item \textbf{\zh{不}} \emph{bù}, not — four separate strokes, and it turns every word you own into its opposite
\end{itemize}

That last one is the largest thing in the chapter. \textbf{\zh{不} does not add one word to your vocabulary; it doubles what you already have.} Everything you have learned to say so far, you have now learned to refuse.

And the two boxes are a down payment of a different kind. \zh{口} and \zh{日} both turn up \textbf{inside} other characters — mouth for speaking and eating, sun for light and time — so the next character that contains one will already be half read.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{口} \zh{日} \zh{不} — name each one, then say what it means
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{日} — and check the middle bar went in before the bottom
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hǎo}, then \textbf{bù hǎo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of this chapter's characters share a shape? (\textbf{\zh{口}} and \textbf{\zh{日}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
